---
title: "Login Node Manners"
---

::: {.quest-dialog}
**Prerequisites:** Grow the Carapace. **Objective:** keep heavy work and sprawling searches off the shared login node and shared storage, and hand heavy work to the scheduler.
**Time:** about 15 minutes. <span class="ao-badge">Last verified (docs, not run): Slurm, Claude Code and OpenCode (V2) docs on 2026-11-16 (sources in `research/hpc-and-notebooks.md`)</span>
:::

Everything below that concerns *etiquette* is **general practice**: the Slurm documentation does not define login nodes, and your site's rules differ. **Follow your own cluster's policy and user guide over this page.** Nothing here says that using an LLM agent on a cluster is allowed or expected. Ask your cluster staff first (see *Keys on Shared Ground*). This quest is read-only: do not run the exercise on a real cluster.

## Login node versus compute node

*General practice.* A login node is shared by everyone who logs in. Compute nodes are where the scheduler places your jobs. Light work (editing text, `git`, listing one directory, checking a log with `head` or `tail`) is normally fine on the login node. Heavy work is not: aligners, long foreground pipelines, compressing or indexing big files, building large environments, or running a test suite at scale.

An agent does not know which node it is on or what your site tolerates. It will happily run a long command if you let it, so the rule is yours to set.

## Shared storage does not like sweeping searches

*General practice.* Network filesystems can slow down for everyone when something touches huge numbers of files. Agents explore by searching, so a careless `find /` or a recursive `grep -r` from your home or project root is the classic mistake. Ask for searches scoped to one subdirectory, and never from `/`.

Claude Code's own search tools (Glob, Grep) are file tools, and its documentation does not describe them as a control on filesystem load. Scoping the search is on you.

## The scheduler's four commands

From the Slurm documentation:

| Command | What it is for |
|---|---|
| `sbatch` | submit a job script for later execution. It returns once the script has a job ID |
| `srun` | run a job or job step in real time. If needed it first creates a resource allocation |
| `squeue` | report the state of jobs |
| `scancel` | cancel a pending or running job |

`sbatch --test-only` validates a script and estimates a start time, and "No job is actually submitted". That makes it a dry run, in the same spirit as the Factory's *Dry Run First*. Slurm's default time limit is the partition's default, so set limits in the script rather than trusting it.

*General practice:* set `--time`, `--mem` and `--cpus-per-task`, and prefer a job array to a loop of `sbatch` calls.

## What the agent's sandbox does and does not cover

- Claude Code's sandbox is shell-only. File tools, MCP servers and hooks run outside it.
- It fails open by default: if it cannot start, commands run **without** sandboxing, unless `sandbox.failIfUnavailable` is `true`. On Linux it needs `bubblewrap` and `socat`. *General practice:* you usually cannot install packages system-wide on a cluster yourself, so a site may have to provide them. Whether it works there is site-specific.
- So "the sandbox is on" is something to check, not assume.

::: {.panel-tabset group="companion"}

## Claude Code

Tell the agent where it may run what, in your project instructions or the prompt, and back it with a permission rule where you can (see *Jobs, Not Jam*). Useful instructions:

- "Search only inside `./workflow/`. Never run `find` or `grep -r` from `/` or `$HOME`."
- "Do not run tools in the foreground. Draft an `sbatch` script and show it to me."

Instructions are guidance, not enforcement.

From the Claude Code docs: foreground commands time out (default 2 minutes, maximum 10 by default), so a long-running foreground command in the agent's shell is cut off anyway.

## OpenCode + Ollama

The same habits apply. OpenCode's documented permission model (V2 docs; check your installed version) ends with allow, ask or deny rules, and an unmatched action asks. Per the docs the base policy begins with an allow-all rule, so `sbatch` is likely to run unprompted; confirm in your version. Add explicit rules for the cluster commands rather than relying on the default. A local model through Ollama does not change anything about which node you are on or how the filesystem behaves.

:::

## Lore

*Further reading. Optional.*

- [Quick Start User Guide](https://slurm.schedmd.com/quickstart.html): SchedMD (Slurm), docs. Why read: it explains sbatch, srun, squeue and scancel; it does not define login-node rules, so read your own site's guide too.
- [Configure permissions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it shows allow, ask and deny rules (for example asking before sbatch) and warns that Bash rules are not a security boundary.
- [sbatch](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html): SchedMD (Slurm), docs. Why read: it is the manual for submitting jobs, including --test-only to validate a request without submitting.
:::
